title: Two Ways to Add Up
statement: How many positive integers less than $500$ can be written as a sum of $4$ consecutive positive integers and can also be written as a sum of $7$ consecutive positive integers? The two lists of consecutive integers need not be related to each other.
hints: Call the first number in each list $a$ or $b$, and write each sum as a simple expression in that letter. Also note the smallest value each sum can take.

Use remainders. The sum of four consecutive integers starting at $a$ is $4a + 6$, which always leaves remainder $2$ on division by $4$. The sum of seven consecutive integers starting at $b$ is $7b + 21$, which is always a multiple of $7$.

Test the multiples of $7$ by their remainders on division by $4$: the numbers that are multiples of $7$ and leave remainder $2$ on division by $4$ are exactly those of the form $14 + 28k$. A sum of seven consecutive positive integers is at least $1 + 2 + \dots + 7 = 28$, so $14$ is too small. It remains to count the allowed values below $500$.
solution: Suppose $N$ is such a number. The four integers starting at $a \ge 1$ have sum $N = a + (a+1) + (a+2) + (a+3) = 4a + 6 = 4(a+1) + 2$, so $N$ leaves remainder $2$ on division by $4$. The seven integers starting at $b \ge 1$ have sum $N = 7b + 21 = 7(b+3)$, so $N$ is a multiple of $7$ and $N \ge 28$. Write $N = 7m$ and $m = 4k + r$ with $r \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$. Then $N = 28k + 7r$, and since $28k$ is a multiple of $4$, the remainder of $N$ on division by $4$ is that of $7r$. The values $7r = 0, 7, 14, 21$ leave remainders $0, 3, 2, 1$ respectively, so only $r = 2$ works. Hence $N = 28k + 14$ for some integer $k \ge 0$, and $N \ge 28$ rules out $k = 0$, so $k \ge 1$. Conversely, every $N = 28k + 14$ with $k \ge 1$ has both forms. Taking $a = 7k + 2$ gives $4a + 6 = 28k + 14$, and taking $b = 4k - 1$ gives $7b + 21 = 28k + 14$. Both starting values are positive integers. So we count the integers $k \ge 1$ with $28k + 14 < 500$, that is, $28k < 486$. Since $28 \cdot 17 = 476$ and $28 \cdot 18 = 504$, this holds exactly for $k = 1, 2, \dots, 17$, giving the values $42, 70, \dots, 490$. The answer is $17$. Why this works. modular-arithmetic, arithmetic-series-sum: writing each sum in terms of its first term turns both conditions into remainder conditions, which combine into one residue modulo $28$.
